Detailed explanation: The provided context shows that sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene leading to the dysfunctional sclerostin protein, which plays a role in regulating bone formation via the Wnt signaling pathway. There is no indication in any of the references that the SOST gene mutation affects the level of a member of the TNF superfamily. Therefore, it is false that Sclerosteosis involves alterations in a TNF superfamily member.

final_answer.text: sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive bone dysplasia characterized by excessive bone growth, severe facial distortion, tall stature, hand malformations (including syndactyly and nail deformities), and raised intracranial pressure
final_answer.long_answer: Reference: [GG_3], [GG_4], [GG_14], [GG_19], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_6]. Detailed explanation: Sclerosteosis is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SOST gene, which encodes the sclerostin protein. The condition is marked by excessive bone formation leading to significant bone overgrowth, particularly evident in the skull, mandible, and tubular bones. Clinical characteristics include severe facial distortion, tall stature, and hand malformations such as syndactyly (fusion of digits) and nail abnormalities. In addition, increased intracranial pressure may occur due to the massive bone growth, which can sometimes lead to compressive neurological complications and, in severe cases, sudden death.

bone.[15] its use has increased bone growth in preclinical trials in osteoporotic rats and monkeys.[29][30] in a phase i study, a single dose of anti-sclerostin antibody from amgen (romosozumab) increased bone density in the hip and spine in healthy men and postmenopausal women and the drug was well tolerated.[31] in a phase ii trial, one year of the antibody treatment in osteoporotic women increased bone density more than bisphosphonate and teriparatide treatment; it had mild injection side effects.[16][32] a phase ii trial of a monoclonal human antibody to sclerostin from eli lilly had positive effects on post-menopausal women. monthly treatments of the antibody for one year increased the bone mineral density of the spine and hip by 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, compared to the placebo group.[33] in a phase iii trial, one year of romosozumab treatment in post-menopausal women reduced the risk of vertebral fractures compared to the placebo group. it also increased the bone mineral density in the lumbar spine (13.3% versus 0.0%), femoral neck (5.2% versus −0.7%) and total hip (6.8% versus 0.0%) compared to the placebo group. adverse events were balanced between the groups.[34] sclerostin has significance within the field of dentistry[35] and  regenerative strategies which target sclerostin are in development.[36] in april 2019, the food and drug administration approved romosozumab for use in women with a very high risk of osteoporotic fracture.[37] it was also approved for use in japan[38] and the european union in 2019.[39]
section: introduction
sclerostin is a protein that in humans is encoded by the sost gene.[5] it is a secreted glycoprotein with a c-terminal cysteine knot-like (ctck) domain and sequence similarity to the dan (differential screening-selected gene aberrative in neuroblastoma) family of bone morphogenetic protein (bmp) antagonists. sclerostin is produced primarily by the osteocyte but is also expressed in other tissues,[6] and has anti-anabolic effects on bone formation.[7]

section: introduction
sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. it was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] it can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] it is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the afrikaner population in south africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of american and brazilian families.[1] recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
section: cause
sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the sost gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] the sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the wnt signaling pathway. wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and rankl synthesis. sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting rankl synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

section: causes
many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, pten mutations such as cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), weaver syndrome, simpson–golabi–behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (m-cmtc) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as noonan syndrome, costello syndrome, gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; fragile x syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as alexander disease, canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and d-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] at one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the section: diagnosis
macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (sds) above the mean.[8] relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two sds above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. if falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  if immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. if a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. benign macrocephaly can occur without reason or be inherited by one or both parents (in which it is considered benign familial macrocephaly and is considered a megalencephaly form of macrocephaly). diagnosis for familial macrocephaly is determined by measuring the head circumference of both parents and comparing it to the child's. benign and familial macrocephaly is not associated with neurological disorders.[10] while benign and familial macrocephaly do not result in neurological disorders, neurodevelopment will still need to be assessed.[citation needed] although neurological disorders do not occur, temporary symptoms of benign and familial macrocephaly include: developmental delay, epilepsy, and mild hypotonia.[10] neurodevelopment is assessed for all cases and suspected cases of macrocephaly to determine whether and what treatments may be needed, and whether any other syndrome/s may be present or likely to develop.[citation needed] other forms of macrocephaly include: macrocephaly at birth: congenital macrocephaly already present at birth.[11] postnatal macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed postnatally (after birth).[12] progressive macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed progressively over time.[13] relative macrocephaly: mild macrocephaly measured under 2 sd from mean, but larger in appearance due to other factors (ex. short stature).[14]

bone.[15] Its use has increased bone growth in preclinical trials in osteoporotic rats and monkeys.[29][30] In a Phase I study, a single dose of anti-sclerostin antibody from Amgen (Romosozumab) increased bone density in the hip and spine in healthy men and postmenopausal women and the drug was well tolerated.[31] In a Phase II trial, one year of the antibody treatment in osteoporotic women increased bone density more than bisphosphonate and teriparatide treatment; it had mild injection side effects.[16][32] A Phase II trial of a monoclonal human antibody to sclerostin from Eli Lilly had positive effects on post-menopausal women. Monthly treatments of the antibody for one year increased the bone mineral density of the spine and hip by 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, compared to the placebo group.[33] In a Phase III trial, one year of Romosozumab treatment in post-menopausal women reduced the risk of vertebral fractures compared to the placebo group. It also increased the bone mineral density in the lumbar spine (13.3% versus 0.0%), femoral neck (5.2% versus −0.7%) and total hip (6.8% versus 0.0%) compared to the placebo group. Adverse events were balanced between the groups.[34] Sclerostin has significance within the field of dentistry[35] and  regenerative strategies which target sclerostin are in development.[36] In April 2019, the Food and Drug Administration approved Romosozumab for use in women with a very high risk of osteoporotic fracture.[37] It was also approved for use in Japan[38] and the European Union in 2019.[39]

llm.short_answer: Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by excessive bone formation in the skull, mandible, and long bones, leading to facial distortion, syndactyly, and potentially increased intracranial pressure.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_2], [GG_12], [GG_16], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2]. Detailed explanation: Sclerosteosis is defined as an autosomal recessive disorder marked by hyperostosis, meaning there is excessive bone formation. This overgrowth is especially prominent in the skull and mandible, with additional involvement of the clavicle, ribs, and the diaphyses of long bones. The accumulation of extra bone can lead to characteristic features including enlargement of the jaw and facial bones that result in facial distortion. Other key features include syndactyly (fusion of digits) and increased intracranial pressure, which can in severe cases lead to sudden death.

Section: Introduction
Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

University of Cape Town determined that a "single mutation" in the gene was responsible for the disorder.[28] An antibody for sclerostin is being developed because of the protein's specificity to bone.[15] Its use has increased bone growth in preclinical trials in osteoporotic rats and monkeys.[29][30] In a Phase I study, a single dose of anti-sclerostin antibody from Amgen (Romosozumab) increased bone density in the hip and spine in healthy men and postmenopausal women and the drug was well tolerated.[31] In a Phase II trial, one year of the antibody treatment in osteoporotic women increased bone density more than bisphosphonate and teriparatide treatment; it had mild injection side effects.[16][32] A Phase II trial of a monoclonal human antibody to sclerostin from Eli Lilly had positive effects on post-menopausal women. Monthly treatments of the antibody for one year increased the bone mineral density of the spine and hip by 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, compared to the placebo group.[33] In a Phase III trial, one year of Romosozumab treatment in post-menopausal women reduced the risk of vertebral fractures compared to the placebo group. It also increased the bone mineral density in the lumbar spine (13.3% versus 0.0%), femoral neck (5.2% versus −0.7%) and total hip (6.8% versus 0.0%) compared to the placebo group. Adverse events were balanced between the groups.[34] Sclerostin has significance within the field of dentistry[35] and  regenerative strategies which target sclerostin are in development.[36] In April 2019, the Food and Drug Administration approved Romosozumab for use in women with a very high risk of osteoporotic fracture.[37] It was also approved for use in Japan[38] and the European Union in 2019.[39]

Detailed explanation: Sclerosteosis is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SOST gene, which encodes the sclerostin protein. The condition is marked by excessive bone formation leading to significant bone overgrowth, particularly evident in the skull, mandible, and tubular bones. Clinical characteristics include severe facial distortion, tall stature, and hand malformations such as syndactyly (fusion of digits) and nail abnormalities. In addition, increased intracranial pressure may occur due to the massive bone growth, which can sometimes lead to compressive neurological complications and, in severe cases, sudden death.

llm.short_answer: An autosomal recessive bone overgrowth disorder characterized by excessive bone formation (especially in the skull, mandible, and tubular bones), facial distortion, syndactyly, and potentially increased intracranial pressure.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_6]. Detailed explanation: Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SOST gene, leading to defective sclerostin production. This results in unchecked Wnt signaling activity, which in turn causes excessive bone formation. Clinically, sclerosteosis is characterized by prominent skeletal overgrowth, with excessive bone formation primarily seen in the skull, mandible, and tubular bones. Common clinical features include facial distortion and syndactyly, and the condition can lead to increased intracranial pressure, which may result in sudden death in severe cases.

Section: Causes
Many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. Pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. Pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. Pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] Many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, PTEN mutations such as Cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), Weaver syndrome, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CMTC) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, Gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; Fragile X syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height Section: Diagnosis
Macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (SDs) above the mean.[8] Relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two SDs above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. If falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  If immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. Diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. If a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. Symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. Benign macrocephaly can occur without reason or be inherited by one or both parents (in which it is considered benign familial macrocephaly and is considered a megalencephaly form of macrocephaly). Diagnosis for familial macrocephaly is determined by measuring the head circumference of both parents and comparing it to the child's. Benign and familial macrocephaly is not associated with neurological disorders.[10] While benign and familial macrocephaly do not result in neurological disorders, neurodevelopment will still need to be assessed.[citation needed] Although neurological disorders do not occur, temporary symptoms of benign and familial macrocephaly include: developmental delay, epilepsy, and mild hypotonia.[10] Neurodevelopment is assessed for all cases and suspected cases of macrocephaly to determine whether and what treatments may be needed, and whether any other syndrome/s may be present or likely to develop.[citation needed] Other forms of macrocephaly include: Macrocephaly at birth: congenital macrocephaly already present at birth.[11] Postnatal macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed postnatally (after birth).[12] Progressive macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed progressively over time.[13] Relative macrocephaly: mild macrocephaly measured under 2 SD from mean, but larger in appearance due to other factors (ex. short stature).[14]

Section: Introduction
Macrocephaly is a condition in which circumference of the human head is abnormally large.[1] It may be pathological or harmless, and can be a familial genetic characteristic. People diagnosed with macrocephaly will receive further medical tests to determine whether the syndrome is accompanied by particular disorders. Those with benign or familial macrocephaly are considered to have megalencephaly.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Sclerosteosis - sclerosteosis
Section: Introduction
Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

llm.short_answer: Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by excessive bone overgrowth primarily in the skull, mandible, and tubular bones, along with features such as facial distortion, syndactyly, and increased intracranial pressure.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_6]. Detailed explanation: Sclerosteosis is a genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern due to mutations in the SOST gene. This mutation leads to reduced inhibition of the Wnt signaling pathway, resulting in excessive bone formation. The condition is marked by pronounced bone overgrowth affecting mainly the skull, mandible, and tubular bones, which can lead to facial distortions and hand malformations (syndactyly). Additionally, the abnormal bone development may result in increased intracranial pressure, potentially causing sudden death.

degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height Macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (SDs) above the mean.[8] Relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two SDs above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. People diagnosed with macrocephaly will receive further medical tests to determine whether the syndrome is accompanied by particular disorders. Section: Causes
Many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. Pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. Pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. Pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] Many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, PTEN mutations such as Cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), Weaver syndrome, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CMTC) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, Gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; Fragile X syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height or brain imaging may be used to determine intracranial volume more accurately.[2] Below is a list of conditions featuring macrocephaly from NCBI's MedGen:[7] Autosomal dominant Kenny-Caffey syndrome B4GALT1-congenital disorder of glycosylation Cobblestone lissencephaly without muscular or ocular involvement Congenital disorder of glycosylation, type Iw, autosomal dominant Corpus callosum, agenesis of Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, autosomal dominant Early-onset parkinsonism-intellectual disability syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type Glutaric aciduria, type 1 Hydrocephalus, nonsyndromic, autosomal recessive Hypophosphatemic rickets and hyperparathyroidism Lethal congenital contracture syndrome MGAT2-congenital disorder of glycosylation Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, Al-Gazali type Niemann-Pick disease, type A Osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis Parietal foramina with cleidocranial dysplasia Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 1A (Zellweger) Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 4B Plasminogen deficiency, type I Severe X-linked myotubular myopathy Sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency Symphalangism with multiple anomalies of hands and feet Syndromic X-linked intellectual disability Thanatophoric dysplasia type 1 Vanishing white matter disease X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia, Chassaing-Lacombe type X-linked intellectual disability with marfanoid habitus
Section: Diagnosis
Macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (SDs) above the mean.[8] Relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two SDs above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. If falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  If immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. Diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. If a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. Symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. Benign macrocephaly can occur without reason or be inherited by one or both parents (in which it is considered benign familial macrocephaly and is considered a megalencephaly form of macrocephaly). Diagnosis for familial macrocephaly is determined by measuring the head circumference of both parents and comparing it to the child's. Benign and familial macrocephaly is not associated with neurological disorders.[10] While benign and familial macrocephaly do not result in neurological disorders, neurodevelopment will still need to be assessed.[citation needed] Although neurological disorders do not occur, temporary symptoms of benign and familial macrocephaly include: developmental delay, epilepsy, and mild hypotonia.[10] Neurodevelopment is assessed for all cases and suspected cases of macrocephaly to determine whether and what treatments may be needed, and whether any other syndrome/s may be present or likely to develop.[citation needed] Other forms of macrocephaly include: Macrocephaly at birth: congenital macrocephaly already present at birth.[11] Postnatal macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed postnatally (after birth).[12] Progressive macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed progressively over time.[13] Relative macrocephaly: mild macrocephaly measured under 2 SD from mean, but larger in appearance due to other factors (ex. short stature).[14]

Section: Introduction
Macrocephaly is a condition in which circumference of the human head is abnormally large.[1] It may be pathological or harmless, and can be a familial genetic characteristic. People diagnosed with macrocephaly will receive further medical tests to determine whether the syndrome is accompanied by particular disorders. Those with benign or familial macrocephaly are considered to have megalencephaly.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Sclerosteosis - sclerosteosis
Section: Introduction
Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Sclerosteosis - sclerosteosis
Section: Introduction
Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

- Reference: [CRAWL_WIKI_1] - Information about: Macrocephaly
Section: Causes
Many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. Pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. Pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. Pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] Many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, PTEN mutations such as Cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), Weaver syndrome, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CMTC) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, Gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; Fragile X syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height or brain imaging may be used to determine intracranial volume more accurately.[2] Below is a list of conditions featuring macrocephaly from NCBI's MedGen:[7] Autosomal dominant Kenny-Caffey syndrome agenesis of Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, autosomal dominant Early-onset parkinsonism-intellectual disability syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type Glutaric aciduria, type 1 Hydrocephalus, nonsyndromic, autosomal recessive Hypophosphatemic rickets and hyperparathyroidism Lethal congenital contracture syndrome MGAT2-congenital disorder of glycosylation Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, Al-Gazali type Niemann-Pick disease, type A Osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis Parietal foramina with cleidocranial dysplasia Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 1A (Zellweger) Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 4B Plasminogen deficiency, type I Severe X-linked myotubular myopathy Sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency Symphalangism with multiple anomalies of hands and feet Syndromic X-linked intellectual disability Thanatophoric dysplasia type 1 Vanishing white matter disease X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia, Chassaing-Lacombe type X-linked intellectual disability with marfanoid habitus
Section: Diagnosis
Macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (SDs) above the mean.[8] Relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two SDs above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. If falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  If immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. Diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. If a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. Symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. Benign macrocephaly can occur without reason or be inherited by one or both parents (in which it is considered benign familial macrocephaly and is considered a megalencephaly form of macrocephaly). Diagnosis for familial macrocephaly is determined by measuring the head circumference of both parents and comparing it to the child's. Benign and familial macrocephaly is not associated with neurological disorders.[10] While benign and familial macrocephaly do not result in neurological disorders, neurodevelopment will still need to be assessed.[citation needed] Although neurological disorders do not occur, temporary symptoms of benign and familial macrocephaly include: developmental delay, epilepsy, and mild hypotonia.[10] Neurodevelopment is assessed for all cases and suspected cases of macrocephaly to determine whether and what treatments may be needed, and whether any other syndrome/s may be present or likely to develop.[citation needed] Other forms of macrocephaly include: Macrocephaly at birth: congenital macrocephaly already present at birth.[11] Postnatal macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed postnatally (after birth).[12] Progressive macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed progressively over time.[13] Relative macrocephaly: mild macrocephaly measured under 2 SD from mean, but larger in appearance due to other factors (ex. short stature).[14]
Section: Associated syndromes
Chromosome 14 - maternal disomy Kelvin Peter anomaly plus syndrome Nevoid basal-cell carcinoma syndrome Osteopathia striata - cranial sclerosis Glutaric aciduria type II Osteopetrosis, autosomal recessive form Short rib syndrome, beemer-langer type Short rib-polydactyly 2 (majewski type) Cobalamin deficiency (combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria) Glutaric aciduria type 1 Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts
Section: Introduction
Macrocephaly is a condition in which circumference of the human head is abnormally large.[1] It may be pathological or harmless, and can be a familial genetic characteristic. People diagnosed with macrocephaly will receive further medical tests to determine whether the syndrome is accompanied by particular disorders. Those with benign or familial macrocephaly are considered to have megalencephaly.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Sclerosteosis - sclerosteosis
Section: Introduction
Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

Section: Causes
Many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. Pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. Pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. Pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] Many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, PTEN mutations such as Cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), Weaver syndrome, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CMTC) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, Gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; Fragile X syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. If falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  If immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. Diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. If a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. Symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. it was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] it can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] it is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the afrikaner population in south africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of american and brazilian families.[1] recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
section: cause
sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the sost gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] the sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the wnt signaling pathway. wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and rankl synthesis. sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting rankl synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

bone.[15] its use has increased bone growth in preclinical trials in osteoporotic rats and monkeys.[29][30] in a phase i study, a single dose of anti-sclerostin antibody from amgen (romosozumab) positive effects on post-menopausal women. monthly treatments of the antibody for one year increased the bone mineral density of the spine and hip by 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, compared groups.[34] sclerostin has significance within the field of dentistry[35] and  regenerative strategies which target sclerostin are in development.[36] in april 2019, the food and drug administration approved romosozumab for use in women with a very high risk of osteoporotic fracture.[37] it was also approved for use in japan[38] and the european union in 2019.[39]
section: introduction
sclerostin is a protein that in humans is encoded by the sost gene.[5] it is a secreted glycoprotein with a c-terminal cysteine knot-like (ctck) domain and sequence similarity to the dan (differential screening-selected gene aberrative in neuroblastoma) family of bone morphogenetic protein (bmp) antagonists. sclerostin is produced primarily by the osteocyte but is also expressed in other tissues,[6] and has anti-anabolic effects on bone formation.[7]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Sclerosteosis - sclerosteosis
Section: Introduction
Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_7] - Information about: Osteocyte - sost gene
Section: Introduction
An osteocyte, an oblate-shaped type of bone cell with dendritic processes, is the most commonly found cell in mature bone. It can live as long as the organism itself.[1] The adult human body has about 42 billion of them.[2]  Osteocytes do not divide and have an average half life of 25 years. They are derived from osteoprogenitor cells, some of which differentiate into active osteoblasts (which may further differentiate to osteocytes).[1] Osteoblasts/osteocytes develop in mesenchyme. In mature bones, osteocytes and their processes reside inside spaces called lacunae (Latin for a pit) and canaliculi, respectively.[1] Osteocytes are simply osteoblasts trapped in the matrix that they secrete. They are networked to each other via long cytoplasmic extensions that occupy tiny canals called canaliculi, which are used for exchange of nutrients and waste through gap junctions. Although osteocytes have reduced synthetic activity and (like osteoblasts) are not capable of mitotic division, they are actively involved in the routine turnover of bony matrix, through various mechanosensory mechanisms. They destroy bone through a rapid, transient (relative to osteoclasts) mechanism called osteocytic osteolysis. Hydroxyapatite, calcium carbonate and calcium phosphate is deposited around the cell.

Section: Introduction
Macrocephaly is a condition in which circumference of the human head is abnormally large.[1] It may be pathological or harmless, and can be a familial genetic characteristic. People diagnosed with macrocephaly will receive further medical tests to determine whether the syndrome is accompanied by particular disorders. Those with benign or familial macrocephaly are considered to have megalencephaly.
Section: Causes
Many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. Pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. Pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. Pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] Many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, PTEN mutations such as Cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), Weaver syndrome, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CMTC) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, Gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; Fragile X syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height or brain imaging may be used to determine intracranial volume more accurately.[2] Below is a list of conditions featuring macrocephaly from NCBI's MedGen:[7] Autosomal dominant Kenny-Caffey syndrome B4GALT1-congenital disorder of glycosylation Cobblestone lissencephaly without muscular or ocular involvement Congenital disorder of glycosylation, type Iw, autosomal dominant Corpus callosum, agenesis of Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, autosomal dominant Early-onset parkinsonism-intellectual disability syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type Glutaric aciduria, type 1 Hydrocephalus, nonsyndromic, autosomal recessive Hypophosphatemic rickets and hyperparathyroidism Lethal congenital contracture syndrome MGAT2-congenital disorder of glycosylation Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, Al-Gazali type Niemann-Pick disease, type A Osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis Parietal foramina with cleidocranial dysplasia Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 1A (Zellweger) Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 4B Plasminogen deficiency, type I Severe X-linked myotubular myopathy Sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency Symphalangism with multiple anomalies of hands and feet Syndromic X-linked intellectual disability Thanatophoric dysplasia type 1 Vanishing white matter disease X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia, Chassaing-Lacombe type X-linked intellectual disability with marfanoid habitus
Section: Diagnosis
Macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (SDs) above the mean.[8] Relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two SDs above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. If falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  If immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. Diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. If a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. Symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. Benign macrocephaly can occur without reason or be inherited by one or both parents (in which it is considered benign familial macrocephaly and is considered a megalencephaly form of macrocephaly). Diagnosis for familial macrocephaly is determined by measuring the head circumference of both parents and comparing it to the child's. Benign and familial macrocephaly is not associated with neurological disorders.[10] While benign and familial macrocephaly do not result in neurological disorders, neurodevelopment will still need to be assessed.[citation needed] Although neurological disorders do not occur, temporary symptoms of benign and familial macrocephaly include: developmental delay, epilepsy, and mild hypotonia.[10] Neurodevelopment is assessed for all cases and suspected cases of macrocephaly to determine whether and what treatments may be needed, and whether any other syndrome/s may be present or likely to develop.[citation needed] Other forms of macrocephaly include: Macrocephaly at birth: congenital macrocephaly already present at birth.[11] Postnatal macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed postnatally (after birth).[12] Progressive macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed progressively over time.[13] Relative macrocephaly: mild macrocephaly measured under 2 SD from mean, but larger in appearance due to other factors (ex. short stature).[14]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Sclerosteosis - sclerosteosis
Section: Introduction
Sclerosteosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_7] - Information about: Osteocyte - sost gene
Section: Introduction
An osteocyte, an oblate-shaped type of bone cell with dendritic processes, is the most commonly found cell in mature bone. It can live as long as the organism itself.[1] The adult human body has about 42 billion of them.[2]  Osteocytes do not divide and have an average half life of 25 years. They are derived from osteoprogenitor cells, some of which differentiate into active osteoblasts (which may further differentiate to osteocytes).[1] Osteoblasts/osteocytes develop in mesenchyme. In mature bones, osteocytes and their processes reside inside spaces called lacunae (Latin for a pit) and canaliculi, respectively.[1] Osteocytes are simply osteoblasts trapped in the matrix that they secrete. They are networked to each other via long cytoplasmic extensions that occupy tiny canals called canaliculi, which are used for exchange of nutrients and waste through gap junctions. Although osteocytes have reduced synthetic activity and (like osteoblasts) are not capable of mitotic division, they are actively involved in the routine turnover of bony matrix, through various mechanosensory mechanisms. They destroy bone through a rapid, transient (relative to osteoclasts) mechanism called osteocytic osteolysis. Hydroxyapatite, calcium carbonate and calcium phosphate is deposited around the cell.

bone.[15] Its use has increased bone growth in preclinical trials in osteoporotic rats and monkeys.[29][30] In a Phase I study, a single dose of anti-sclerostin antibody from Amgen (Romosozumab) positive effects on post-menopausal women. Monthly treatments of the antibody for one year increased the bone mineral density of the spine and hip by 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, compared to the placebo group.[33] In a Phase III trial, one year of Romosozumab treatment in post-menopausal women reduced the risk of vertebral fractures compared to the placebo group. It was first described in 1958[1][2] but given the current name in 1967.[3] Excessive bone formation is most prominent in the skull, mandible and tubular bones.[1] It can cause facial distortion and syndactyly.[1] Increased intracranial pressure can cause sudden death in patients.[1] It is a rare disorder that is most prominent in the Afrikaner population in South Africa (40 patients), but there have also been cases of American and Brazilian families.[1] Recently, porcupine inhibition has emerged as a promising pharmacological treatment for severe sclerosteosis pathologies, and is currently in preclinical research.[4]
Section: Cause
Sclerosteosis is caused by mutations in the SOST gene that encodes the sclerostin protein.[5] The sclerostin protein is necessary in inhibiting the Wnt signaling pathway. Wnt signalling results in increased osteoblast activity and RANKL synthesis. Sclerostin therefore increases bone formation by indirectly inhibiting RANKL synthesis and thus osteoclast activation.

University of Cape Town determined that a "single mutation" in the gene was responsible for the disorder.[28] An antibody for sclerostin is being developed because of the protein's specificity to bone.[15] Its use has increased bone growth in preclinical trials in osteoporotic rats and monkeys.[29][30] In a Phase I study, a single dose of anti-sclerostin antibody from Amgen (Romosozumab) increased bone density in the hip and spine in healthy men and postmenopausal women and the drug was well tolerated.[31] In a Phase II trial, one year of the antibody treatment in osteoporotic women increased bone density more than bisphosphonate and teriparatide treatment; it had mild injection side effects.[16][32] A Phase II trial of a monoclonal human antibody to sclerostin from Eli Lilly had positive effects on post-menopausal women. Monthly treatments of the antibody for one year increased the bone mineral density of the spine and hip by 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, compared to the placebo group.[33] In a Phase III trial, one year of Romosozumab treatment in post-menopausal women reduced the risk of vertebral fractures compared to the placebo group. It also increased the bone mineral density in the lumbar spine (13.3% versus 0.0%), femoral neck (5.2% versus −0.7%) and total hip (6.8% versus 0.0%) compared to the placebo group. Adverse events were balanced between the groups.[34] Sclerostin has significance within the field of dentistry[35] and  regenerative strategies which target sclerostin are in development.[36] In April 2019, the Food and Drug Administration approved Romosozumab for use in women with a very high risk of osteoporotic fracture.[37] It was also approved for use in Japan[38] and the European Union in 2019.[39]
Section: Introduction

Sclerostin is produced primarily by the osteocyte but is also expressed in other tissues,[6] and has anti-anabolic effects on bone formation.[7]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_4] - Information about: Macrocephaly - sclerosteosis
Section: Introduction
Macrocephaly is a condition in which circumference of the human head is abnormally large.[1] It may be pathological or harmless, and can be a familial genetic characteristic. People diagnosed with macrocephaly will receive further medical tests to determine whether the syndrome is accompanied by particular disorders. Those with benign or familial macrocephaly are considered to have megalencephaly.
Section: Causes
Many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. Pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. Pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. Pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] Many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, PTEN mutations such as Cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), Weaver syndrome, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CMTC) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, Gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; Fragile X syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height or brain imaging may be used to determine intracranial volume more accurately.[2] Below is a list of conditions featuring macrocephaly from NCBI's MedGen:[7] Autosomal dominant Kenny-Caffey syndrome B4GALT1-congenital disorder of glycosylation Cobblestone lissencephaly without muscular or ocular involvement Congenital disorder of glycosylation, type Iw, autosomal dominant Corpus callosum, agenesis of Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, autosomal dominant Early-onset parkinsonism-intellectual disability syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type Glutaric aciduria, type 1 Hydrocephalus, nonsyndromic, autosomal recessive Hypophosphatemic rickets and hyperparathyroidism Lethal congenital contracture syndrome MGAT2-congenital disorder of glycosylation Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, Al-Gazali type Niemann-Pick disease, type A Osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis Parietal foramina with cleidocranial dysplasia Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 1A (Zellweger) Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 4B Plasminogen deficiency, type I Severe X-linked myotubular myopathy Sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency Symphalangism with multiple anomalies of hands and feet Syndromic X-linked intellectual disability Thanatophoric dysplasia type 1 Vanishing white matter disease X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia, Chassaing-Lacombe type X-linked intellectual disability with marfanoid habitus
Section: Diagnosis
Macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (SDs) above the mean.[8] Relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two SDs above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. If falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  If immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. Diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. If a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. Symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. Benign macrocephaly can occur without reason or be inherited by one or both parents (in which it is considered benign familial macrocephaly and is considered a megalencephaly form of macrocephaly). Diagnosis for familial macrocephaly is determined by measuring the head circumference of both parents and comparing it to the child's. Benign and familial macrocephaly is not associated with neurological disorders.[10] While benign and familial macrocephaly do not result in neurological disorders, neurodevelopment will still need to be assessed.[citation needed] Although neurological disorders do not occur, temporary symptoms of benign and familial macrocephaly include: developmental delay, epilepsy, and mild hypotonia.[10] Neurodevelopment is assessed for all cases and suspected cases of macrocephaly to determine whether and what treatments may be needed, and whether any other syndrome/s may be present or likely to develop.[citation needed] Other forms of macrocephaly include: Macrocephaly at birth: congenital macrocephaly already present at birth.[11] Postnatal macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed postnatally (after birth).[12] Progressive macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed progressively over time.[13] Relative macrocephaly: mild macrocephaly measured under 2 SD from mean, but larger in appearance due to other factors (ex. short stature).[14]
Section: Associated syndromes
Below is a list of syndromes associated with macrocephaly that are noted in Signs and Symptoms of Genetic Conditions: A Handbook.[10] Chromosome 14 - maternal disomy Kelvin Peter anomaly plus syndrome Nevoid basal-cell carcinoma syndrome Osteopathia striata - cranial sclerosis Glutaric aciduria type II Osteopetrosis, autosomal recessive form Short rib syndrome, beemer-langer type Short rib-polydactyly 2 (majewski type) Cobalamin deficiency (combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria) Glutaric aciduria type 1 Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_7] - Information about: Osteocyte - sost gene
Section: Introduction
An osteocyte, an oblate-shaped type of bone cell with dendritic processes, is the most commonly found cell in mature bone. It can live as long as the organism itself.[1] The adult human body has about 42 billion of them.[2]  Osteocytes do not divide and have an average half life of 25 years. They are derived from osteoprogenitor cells, some of which differentiate into active osteoblasts (which may further differentiate to osteocytes).[1] Osteoblasts/osteocytes develop in mesenchyme. In mature bones, osteocytes and their processes reside inside spaces called lacunae (Latin for a pit) and canaliculi, respectively.[1] Osteocytes are simply osteoblasts trapped in the matrix that they secrete. They are networked to each other via long cytoplasmic extensions that occupy tiny canals called canaliculi, which are used for exchange of nutrients and waste through gap junctions. Although osteocytes have reduced synthetic activity and (like osteoblasts) are not capable of mitotic division, they are actively involved in the routine turnover of bony matrix, through various mechanosensory mechanisms. They destroy bone through a rapid, transient (relative to osteoclasts) mechanism called osteocytic osteolysis. Hydroxyapatite, calcium carbonate and calcium phosphate is deposited around the cell.

Section: Introduction
Macrocephaly is a condition in which circumference of the human head is abnormally large.[1] It may be pathological or harmless, and can be a familial genetic characteristic. People diagnosed with macrocephaly will receive further medical tests to determine whether the syndrome is accompanied by particular disorders. Those with benign or familial macrocephaly are considered to have megalencephaly.
Section: Causes
Many people with abnormally large heads or large skulls are healthy, but macrocephaly may be pathological. Pathologic macrocephaly may be due to megalencephaly (enlarged brain), hydrocephalus (abnormally increased cerebrospinal fluid), cranial hyperostosis (bone overgrowth), and other conditions. Pathologic macrocephaly is called "syndromic", when it is associated with any other noteworthy condition, and "nonsyndromic" otherwise. Pathologic macrocephaly may be caused by congenital anatomic abnormalities, genetic conditions, or by environmental events.[2] Many genetic conditions are associated with macrocephaly, including familial macrocephaly related to the holgate gene, autism, PTEN mutations such as Cowden disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis; overgrowth syndromes such as Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism), Weaver syndrome, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (bulldog syndrome), and macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CMTC) syndrome; neurocardiofacial-cutaneous syndromes such as Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome, Gorlin syndrome,[3] (also known as basal cell nevus syndrome) and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome; Fragile X syndrome; leukodystrophies (brain white matter degeneration) such as Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; and glutaric aciduria type 1 and D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria.[2] At one end of the genetic spectrum, duplications of chromosomes have been found to be related to autism and macrocephaly; at the other end, deletions of chromosomes have been found to be related to schizophrenia and microcephaly.[4][5][6] Environmental events associated with macrocephaly include infection, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding within the infant brain), subdural hematoma (bleeding beneath the outer lining of the brain), subdural effusion (collection of fluid beneath the outer lining of the brain), and arachnoid cysts (cysts on the brain surface).[2] In research, cranial height or brain imaging may be used to determine intracranial volume more accurately.[2] Below is a list of conditions featuring macrocephaly from NCBI's MedGen:[7] Autosomal dominant Kenny-Caffey syndrome B4GALT1-congenital disorder of glycosylation Cobblestone lissencephaly without muscular or ocular involvement Congenital disorder of glycosylation, type Iw, autosomal dominant Corpus callosum, agenesis of Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, autosomal dominant Early-onset parkinsonism-intellectual disability syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type Glutaric aciduria, type 1 Hydrocephalus, nonsyndromic, autosomal recessive Hypophosphatemic rickets and hyperparathyroidism Lethal congenital contracture syndrome MGAT2-congenital disorder of glycosylation Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, Al-Gazali type Niemann-Pick disease, type A Osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis Parietal foramina with cleidocranial dysplasia Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 1A (Zellweger) Peroxisome biogenesis disorder 4B Plasminogen deficiency, type I Severe X-linked myotubular myopathy Sulfite oxidase deficiency due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency Symphalangism with multiple anomalies of hands and feet Syndromic X-linked intellectual disability Thanatophoric dysplasia type 1 Vanishing white matter disease X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia, Chassaing-Lacombe type X-linked intellectual disability with marfanoid habitus
Section: Diagnosis
Macrocephaly is customarily diagnosed if head circumference is greater than two standard deviations (SDs) above the mean.[8] Relative macrocephaly occurs if the measure is less than two SDs above the mean, but is disproportionately above that when ethnicity and stature are considered. Diagnosis can be determined in utero or can be determined within 18–24 months after birth in some cases where head circumference tends to stabilize in infants.[9] Diagnosis in infants includes measuring the circumference of the child's head and comparing how significant it falls above the 97.5 percentile of children similar to their demographic. If falling above the 97.5th percentile then the patient will be checked to determine whether there is any intracranial pressure present and whether or not immediate surgery is needed.[10]  If immediate surgery is not needed then further testing will be done to determine whether the patient has either macrocephaly or benign macrocephaly. Diagnosis for macrocephaly involves the comparison of the infant's head circumference to that of other infants of the same age and ethnicity. If a patient is suspected of having macrocephaly molecular testing will be used to confirm diagnosis. Symptoms vary on the cause of macrocephaly on the child and if the child has any other accompanying syndromes which will be determined through molecular testing. Benign macrocephaly can occur without reason or be inherited by one or both parents (in which it is considered benign familial macrocephaly and is considered a megalencephaly form of macrocephaly). Diagnosis for familial macrocephaly is determined by measuring the head circumference of both parents and comparing it to the child's. Benign and familial macrocephaly is not associated with neurological disorders.[10] While benign and familial macrocephaly do not result in neurological disorders, neurodevelopment will still need to be assessed.[citation needed] Although neurological disorders do not occur, temporary symptoms of benign and familial macrocephaly include: developmental delay, epilepsy, and mild hypotonia.[10] Neurodevelopment is assessed for all cases and suspected cases of macrocephaly to determine whether and what treatments may be needed, and whether any other syndrome/s may be present or likely to develop.[citation needed] Other forms of macrocephaly include: Macrocephaly at birth: congenital macrocephaly already present at birth.[11] Postnatal macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed postnatally (after birth).[12] Progressive macrocephaly: macrocephaly developed progressively over time.[13] Relative macrocephaly: mild macrocephaly measured under 2 SD from mean, but larger in appearance due to other factors (ex. short stature).[14]

Below is a list of syndromes associated with macrocephaly that are noted in Signs and Symptoms of Genetic Conditions: A Handbook.[10] Chromosome 14 - maternal disomy Kelvin Peter anomaly plus syndrome Nevoid basal-cell carcinoma syndrome Osteopathia striata - cranial sclerosis Glutaric aciduria type II Osteopetrosis, autosomal recessive form Short rib syndrome, beemer-langer type Short rib-polydactyly 2 (majewski type) Cobalamin deficiency (combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria) Glutaric aciduria type 1 Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts
